out.other_title: Performance gap recovered (PGR) metric for weak-to-strong generalization
out.rationale: Burns et al. define performance gap recovered relative to a weak-supervisor baseline and a strong ceiling; the authors explicitly build on that framework but define PR as a ratio to the Pass@N oracle, without a weak-model baseline. PR scores Best-of-N sampling guided by reward models trained on critics' judgments (in the Figure 3 setting, on a fixed 7B supervised model with critic models of varying sizes, which the passage does not say are weaker), whereas PGR scores a weak-to-strong model trained with weak supervision against the weak supervisor and the strong ceiling.
out.scope: proposed EXTENDS: How to measure how much of a model's achievable performance a supervision signal recovers; Burns et al. use weak supervision, while the authors use reward models trained on the judgments of critics of varying sizes.

text: To quantify supervision effectiveness, the authors adopt a Performance Recovered (PR) metric 'following the framework established by' Burns et al. (2023). Reward models trained on critics' judgments guide Best-of-N sampling, and PR compares this Best-of-N performance against the oracle Pass@N: the expected r* of the sample selected by maximizing r over n samples, divided by the expected maximum of r* over those samples.
title: Wen et al. adopt a Best-of-N Performance Recovered (PR) metric following Burns et al.'s framework
